Introduction
What is geology?
The study of the history, composition and make-up of the Earth
The study of the weather and climate of an area
The study of the stars, planets and galaxies
The study of plants and the soils they grow in
The manual defines geology as the study of the history, composition and make-up of the Earth.
Introduction
According to the manual, what do the rocks of an area determine?
The type of soils in that area
The amount of rain in that area
The temperature of that area
The direction rivers flow in
Rocks determine the type of soils and that, combined with climate, are the main factors determining the flora and fauna.
The formation of the Earth
Why did the Earth become spherical in shape?
Its strong, evenly distributed gravitational pull towards the centre
The fast spinning of the Earth on its axis
Erosion of the land surfaces over millions of years
The pull of the sun's gravity on the Earth
The molten Earth was malleable and the evenly distributed gravitational pull towards the centre made it spherical.
The Earth's structure
Which heavy metals were drawn towards the Earth's centre by gravity?
Iron and nickel
Aluminium and magnesium
Gold and silver
Copper and tin
Gravity drew heavier metals like iron and nickel towards the centre, while lighter aluminium and magnesium stayed near the surface.

What fractures the Earth's crust into plates?
Currents caused by heat in the semi-liquid mantle
Earthquakes caused by the moon's gravity
Erosion of the crust by wind and water
The cooling and shrinking of the inner core
The heat in the semi-liquid part of the mantle generates currents that fracture the Earth's crust into plates.

Which layer of the Earth is a dense liquid made of an iron-nickel alloy?

The inner core
The mantle
The crust

How thick is the Earth's crust, according to the manual?
7 to 35 km

The Kunyere fault

The Pan-handle fault

Which two African plates are drifting apart along the Great Rift Valley?

The Kalahari and Zimbabwe plates
The Nubian and Kalahari plates
The Somali and Zambezi plates

Geological features in Botswana
How were the Gcwhihaba Caves (including Drotsky's Caves) created?
Water containing carbon dioxide dissolved the limestone
Lava flows cooled and left hollow tubes
Wind blew sand against the rocks
Earthquakes cracked open the quartzite
The caves were created when water containing carbon dioxide seeped through limestone, dissolving the rock.

What type of rock are the Tsodilo Hills made of?
Quartzite, a metamorphic rock
Granite, an igneous rock
Dolomite, a sedimentary rock
Rhyolite, a volcanic rock

What is the origin of the Savuti Hills?

Sedimentary (layers of sandstone)

Organic (old coral beds)

Geological features in Botswana
The Otse Hills on Botswana's southern border are mainly made of which rock?
Sedimentary sandstone
Volcanic rhyolite
Metamorphic quartzite
Dolomite and marble

Formation of the Kalahari Basin
What event led to the formation of the Kalahari Basin?
South America separating from Africa
The Drakensberg Mountains being pushed up
The drying up of the Makgadikgadi super-lake
A huge volcano collapsing in the interior
The Kalahari Basin formed from tectonic movements when South America separated from Africa, causing a recoil.
Formation of the Kalahari Basin
Why is Kalahari sand very poor in nutrients?
Its granitic origin and millions of years of leaching by rain
It is too young for minerals to have formed in it
It comes from volcanic rock that has no minerals
Animals have eaten all the plants that held nutrients
Due to the granitic origin of the sand and leaching by rain over hundreds of millions of years, it is very poor in nutrients.
Formation of the Kalahari Basin
What does the manual say makes the Kalahari sands special?
They are the largest continuous body of sand in the world
They are the deepest sands in the world
They are the youngest sands in Africa
They are the most fertile sands in Africa
The Kalahari sands span from the Cape Province to the Congo, the largest continuous body of sand in the world.
Formation of the Makgadikgadi
What caused the formation of the Paleo-Lake Makgadikgadi?
A sudden uplift of the Zimbabwe-Kalahari Axis
The separation of South America from Africa
Heavy rains over the Bié Plateau
The collapse of the Great Rift Valley
The sudden uplift of the Zimbabwe-Kalahari Axis about 2 million years ago blocked the rivers and formed the super-lake.
Formation of the Makgadikgadi
What was the approximate size of the Makgadikgadi super-lake?
About 200 000 km²
About 20 000 km²
About 2 000 km²
About 2 000 000 km²

When did the Makgadikgadi super-lake finally dry up?
Around 10 000 years ago
Around 2 million years ago
Around 100 years ago
Around 900 million years ago
The uplift of the Thamalakane and Kunyere fault-lines cut off its water and the super-lake finally dried up around 10 000 years ago.
Formation of the Makgadikgadi
How were the Makgadikgadi Salt Pans formed?
Salts and minerals concentrated as the lake dried up
Sea water flooded the area and then evaporated
Volcanic ash settled over the old lake bed
Wind blew salt in from the Atlantic Ocean
The drying of the lake concentrated the salts and minerals; once fully dried, these deposits formed the salt pans.

The lava cools quickly on the surface
They are formed from layers of sand
They are changed by heat and pressure
Intrusive igneous rock solidifies underground, so it cools slowly, resulting in larger crystals.

Which is a typical intrusive igneous rock?
Granite
Basalt
Shale
Schist

Rocks
How are metamorphic rocks formed?
Existing rocks are changed by heat, pressure or fluids without melting
Magma cools and hardens on or below the surface
Particles settle in layers and are cemented together
Shells, corals and skeletons build up on the sea floor

Shale
Granite
Sandstone
Limestone

Crystals
Faults
Exfoliation

Sand particles (coarse material)
Coral beds and shells
Cooled lava

Basalt

Rocks
Why do coal, gas and oil not contain minerals?

They are formed from cooled magma
They are formed under extreme pressure

Rock cycles

They become igneous rocks straight away
They break down into sand
They turn into fossil fuels
When sedimentary rocks are exposed to great heat and pressure they become metamorphic.
Weathering
What is weathering?
The breaking down of rocks in situ (where they are)
The movement of rock particles by wind and water
The settling of particles into layers
The melting of rock deep underground
Weathering is the process of breaking down rocks, in situ, through water, plants and the atmosphere.
Weathering
Water combining with iron minerals in a rock (rusting) is an example of what?
Chemical weathering
Mechanical weathering
Biotic weathering
Wind erosion
Oxidation or rusting, where water combines with iron minerals in the rock, is a form of chemical weathering.
Weathering

Mechanical weathering
Chemical weathering
Biotic weathering
Water erosion

Weathering
The rock-splitting fig growing roots into a crack is a typical example of what?
Biotic weathering
Chemical weathering
Pressure release
Water erosion
Biotic weathering includes plants growing in cracks in rock; the rock-splitting fig is the typical example.
Erosion
What is erosion?
The active movement of rock particles by wind and water
The breaking down of rocks where they lie
The cementing of particles into rock
The changing of rock by heat and pressure
Erosion is the active movement of rock particles by wind and water, linking weathering and deposition.
Erosion
